## Start a project

| What you want | Command |
|------------|------------------------|
| Make a project from the course template (it asks you questions) | `pixi exec --spec cookiecutter --spec git -- cookiecutter gh:khan-lab/cbio7501-f26 --directory templates/cookiecutter-repro-project` |
| The same without questions | add `--no-input` and the answers as `key="value"`, e.g. `project_slug="ltee-project" license="MIT"` |

```{.bash}
find . -type d | sort      # see the folders it made
```

Taught in [lesson 02, section 3](../pages/02-project-organization.qmd#generate-the-project-from-the-template).

## Where things go

| Folder or file | What goes in it | In Git? |
|----------------|-----------------|---------|
| `data/raw/` | downloaded data: read-only, never edited | no (only its README) |
| `data/processed/` | data made from the raw data by code | no |
| `metadata/` | sample sheet, data sources, checksums | yes |
| `scripts/` | code, run from the project folder | yes |
| `config/`, `workflow/` | settings, and the Snakemake and Nextflow workflows | yes |
| `notebooks/` | Jupyter notebooks for exploring, outputs cleared | yes |
| `reports/` | the Quarto report | yes (not the rendered HTML) |
| `results/` | everything code makes: delete and rebuild any time | no (only its README) |
| `docs/` | notes, decision log, project structure | yes |
| `envs/`, `containers/` | Conda export files, Dockerfile, Apptainer recipe | yes (not saved images) |
| `pixi.toml`, `pixi.lock` | the software: what you asked for, and exactly what was installed | yes |

: {tbl-colwidths="[25,55,20]"}

See [lesson 02, section 4](../pages/02-project-organization.qmd#walk-through-the-layout).

## Rules worth keeping

- Run everything from the project folder, with paths relative to it (`metadata/samples.tsv`, never `/Users/ada/...`).
- Raw data is downloaded by code and read-only; processed data and results are rebuilt by code.
- Name files so they sort and can be read by programs: no spaces, ISO dates (`2026-10-25`), leading zeros (`sample-01`), the same order of parts every time.
- Start the README on day one.

## Get and check data

| What you want | Command |
|------------|------------------------|
| Download a file, retrying on network errors | `curl -L --fail --retry 5 --retry-all-errors -o FILE URL` |
| Unpack a `.tar.gz` archive | `tar -xzf FILE.tar.gz -C FOLDER` |
| Look at the first read of a FASTQ file | `head -4 FILE.fastq` |
| Record checksums of the files you keep | `sha256sum data/raw/fastq/*.fastq data/raw/reference/*.gz > metadata/checksums.sha256` |
| Check every file against them | `sha256sum -c metadata/checksums.sha256` (older macOS: `shasum -a 256 -c ...`) |
| Make raw data read-only | `chmod a-w data/raw/fastq/* data/raw/reference/*` |
| Make one file writable again, to replace it | `chmod u+w FILE` |
| Download and verify everything, the project's way | `pixi exec python scripts/download_data.py` (from lesson 05: `pixi run download`) |
| Only verify | `pixi exec python scripts/download_data.py --verify-only` |

```{.bash}
# Check a download against the MD5 its provider published (two spaces before the file name)
echo "MD5  FILE" | md5sum -c -
# Look into a gzipped file
gunzip -c FILE.gz | head -1
```

Taught in [lesson 03, Part B](../pages/03-data-management.qmd#hands-on).

## FAIR in one line each

| | In practice |
|-|-------------|
| **F**indable | a persistent identifier (a DOI from Zenodo or figshare, an SRA or ENA accession) and rich metadata |
| **A**ccessible | an open, standard download (HTTPS), or a clear procedure for controlled access |
| **I**nteroperable | open formats (FASTQ, VCF, CSV/TSV) and shared vocabularies |
| **R**eusable | a license (CC0 or CC BY), provenance, and a README that says how the data was made |

FAIR is not the same as open. See [lesson 03, Part A](../pages/03-data-management.qmd#fair-in-one-table).

## CARE in one line each

For data from Indigenous Peoples and their lands, used together with FAIR:

| | In practice |
|-|-------------|
| **C**ollective benefit | the communities the data comes from benefit from its use; results go back to them |
| **A**uthority to control | community agreement as well as individual consent; the community has a say in access |
| **R**esponsibility | report back how the data was used; build lasting relationships |
| **E**thics | weigh harms to the group, not only to individuals; record limits on future use in the metadata |

FAIR asks whether data can be used; CARE asks for whom and who decides. See
[lesson 03, Part A](../pages/03-data-management.qmd#care-in-one-table).

## Official cheat sheets and references

There is no official cheat sheet for organizing projects or managing data.
These are the references the lessons build on:

- Cookiecutter, *Usage* (how templates are found and filled in): <https://cookiecutter.readthedocs.io/en/stable/usage.html>
- The course template and its README: <https://github.com/khan-lab/cbio7501-f26/tree/main/templates/cookiecutter-repro-project>
- Wilson G et al. (2017). Good enough practices in scientific computing. *PLoS Comput Biol* 13:e1005510. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005510>
- Wilkinson MD et al. (2016). The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship. *Sci Data* 3:160018. <https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18>
- Global Indigenous Data Alliance, *CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance*: <https://www.gida-global.org/careprinciples>
- Carroll SR et al. (2020). The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance. *Data Sci J* 19:43. <https://doi.org/10.5334/dsj-2020-043>
- The Carpentries Incubator, *FAIR in (biological) practice*: <https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/fair-bio-practice/>
